subject: maths
title: Circle theorems

slides.heading: Circle theorems — angle rules that come from the circle's symmetry
slides.body: A set of angle rules governs triangles and quadrilaterals drawn inside or on circles — these are circle theorems, and they all follow from the symmetry of the circle. You need to recognise the geometric setup in a diagram (e.g. two radii forming a triangle, an angle at the centre vs the circumference) before you can apply the correct rule. Being able to state the theorem you used — not just give the angle — is essential for full marks.
slides.note: Maximum 3 sentences. Plain English. No AQA references. What is this and why does it matter.

slides.heading: Circle measurements and key theorems
slides.formula: Circumference = πd  or  2πr  |  Area = πr²  |  Angle at centre = 2 × angle at circumference (same arc)  |  Angle in a semicircle = 90°  |  Angles in the same segment are equal  |  Opposite angles of a cyclic quadrilateral add to 180°  |  Tangent is perpendicular to radius at the point of contact
slides.formulaExplained: For a circle of radius r (or diameter d = 2r): circumference is the distance all the way round (πd or equivalently 2πr); area is the flat space inside (πr²). For angle theorems: an angle at the centre is exactly double the angle at the circumference when both are subtended by the same arc. An angle inscribed in a semicircle is always 90°. Two angles in the same segment (same side of a chord) are equal. In a cyclic quadrilateral (all four vertices on the circle), opposite angles add to 180°. A tangent meets the radius at exactly 90°.
slides.whenToUse: Any question involving a circle diagram with points on the circumference, angles at the centre, chords, tangents, or a cyclic quadrilateral. State the theorem by name in your working.
slides.note: Show formula in standard notation. Explain each variable. State when this formula applies.

slides.heading: Let's work through one
slides.question: O is the centre of a circle. Points A and B are on the circumference. The angle AOB at the centre is 112°. Find the angle ACB at the circumference, where C is another point on the major arc.

steps.instruction: Identify the theorem. Angle AOB is at the centre; angle ACB is at the circumference — both are subtended by arc AB. This is the angle at the centre theorem.
steps.working: Angle at centre = 2 × angle at circumference

steps.instruction: Rearrange to find the circumference angle.
State the answer with the reason.
steps.working: Angle ACB = 56° (angle at the centre is twice the angle at the circumference, subtended by the same arc).

slides.note: Numbers must differ from any question in the question bank for this subtopic.

slides.heading: Watch out for this

mistakes.mistake: Doubling the circumference angle to get the centre angle instead of halving the centre angle — getting 224° instead of 56°.
mistakes.correction: The centre angle is the larger one: centre = 2 × circumference. If you're finding the circumference angle, divide the centre angle by 2, not multiply.

mistakes.mistake: Using the circumference formula (2πr) for area, or the area formula (πr²) for circumference — mixing up the two.
mistakes.correction: Circumference = distance around the edge → 2πr or πd (one factor of r). Area = space inside → πr² (r squared). The squared symbol in πr² is the trigger: that formula gives area.

mistakes.mistake: Not stating the theorem used — just writing the angle without justification.
mistakes.correction: In circle theorem questions, the reason is worth marks. Write the full theorem name: e.g. 'angle in a semicircle = 90°' or 'opposite angles of a cyclic quadrilateral sum to 180°'.

slides.note: Minimum 2, maximum 3 mistakes. Specific not generic.

keyFacts.fact: Circumference = πd = 2πr. Area = πr². These are two different quantities — circumference is the perimeter (linear), area is the space inside (squared units).
keyFacts.examTip: If a question gives a diameter, halve it to get r before using A = πr². Using d instead of r in the area formula gives an answer four times too large.

keyFacts.fact: Angle at the centre = 2 × angle at the circumference (same arc). Angle in a semicircle = 90°.
keyFacts.examTip: The semicircle rule is a special case of the centre theorem: the angle at the centre is 180° (a diameter), so the circumference angle is 90°.

keyFacts.fact: Opposite angles in a cyclic quadrilateral add to 180°. Angles in the same segment are equal.
keyFacts.examTip: Draw the chord that creates the segment — angles in the same segment are on the same side of that chord. If they're on opposite sides, they are supplementary (add to 180°), not equal.

note: keyFacts: 2-4 entries. Exam-precise language. These are what Mabel writes into her notes.
